truthfulness. ∎
public_text.7:
Up to the irrelevant tax term the choice problem is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),\qquad 
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),$$

so that for the two admissible technologies

$$ {\cal P}(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
{\cal P}(\theta ,1)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta),\qquad p_{1}:=p(1)>0, $$

and

$$\Delta(\theta):={\cal P}(\theta,1)-{\cal P}(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)\ge 0,
\qquad \Delta(1)=0 .$$

On the interior $0\le\theta<1$ we have $1-\theta>0$ and $F(\theta)>0$ both
decreasing, hence

$$m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$$

is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and

$$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p_{1}\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
 \qquad 0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,$$

so the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded as truthfulness rises.
In particular

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ therefore strictly
dominates the strict auditor $x=1$ on the whole interior of the type
support, and the dominance is monotone in $\theta$ : the gain from
avoiding the no-report event,

$$\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)>0,$$

is positive and strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  Hence the (unique)
best reply on the interior is flat,

$$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference only in the limit $\theta\to1$ where the refusal
probability $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes and ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.
In the usual continuum language this is the interior regime
$0<\theta<1$, i.e. $\theta\in[0,1)$ up to the inessential boundary
indifference at $\theta=1$: a marginal increase in truthfulness
strictly reduces the expected cost of a strict auditor while leaving the
cost of a lenient auditor unchanged, so the firm stays with – and in
the limit becomes essentially indifferent between – the more lenient
choice. The familiar statement is that the strict preference for
leniency holds for every $\theta<1$, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$, and is
exhausted at the truthful limit $\theta=1$ where the auditor becomes
irrelevant.  That is the non-trivial monotone region commonly reported
as $0<\theta<1$, i.e. the whole interior where higher truthfulness is
associated with the weakly more lenient, and in the strict interior
uniquely lenient, best reply.
public_text.4:
I think we all agree on the algebra.  Up to the $t(\theta)$ term

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta ),$$

so with the two admissible auditors

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta )+(1-\theta )p(1)F(\theta ),$$

and

$$\Delta C(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,$$

with $\Delta C(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and $\Delta C(1)=0$.  $m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is decreasing on the support, so the incremental expected penalty created by a refusal,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and is $>0$ on the interior.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1).$$

Up to the irrelevant $t(\theta)$ the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every $\theta<1$, and the best reply is flat $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference at the top.

The strict comparative static $ \theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ is therefore absent on the interior, because $x^{*}$ is constant on $[0,1)$.  The only place where an increase in truthfulness can be associated with a (weak) move toward leniency is the boundary where the refusal risk disappears.  At $\theta=1$ we have $x(1-\theta)=0$, so ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and the firm is indifferent between $x=0$ and $x=1$.  With the common belief in the statement that a major reputable audit makes a second Revenue Service audit unlikely, $p(1)<p(0)$, the residual refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ is the only cost left to the firm once $\theta$ is close to one.  Breaking the tie at the top in the usual way, i.e. eliminating any residual refusal risk, the truthful type $\theta=1$ is the type that can afford to switch to the lenient technology at zero cost.

In the discrete two-point model this is the degenerate indifference point $\theta=1$; in the continuum description it is the weak preference for leniency on $[0,1)$ with exhaustion at $\theta=1$.  That is the usual statement that the incentive to avoid a strict auditor, $\Delta C(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is decreasing in truthfulness, so the (weak) move toward leniency is realised only at the top of the type space, essentially $\theta=1$, the limit of the strict preference region $[0,1)$.  The interior monotone strict decrease $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty, the non-trivial weak effect being concentrated at the indifference boundary.
public_text.6:
The cost that is really driving the auditor choice is the part that depends on $x$,

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta ),
\qquad C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+{\cal P}(\theta ,x),
$$

up to the $x$-independent tax $t(\theta)$.  For the two admissible
technologies

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
{\cal P}(\theta ,1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta )\ge 0,
$$

so that with $p_{1}=p(1)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta):={\cal P}(\theta ,1)-{\cal P}(\theta ,0)
            =(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta ),\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  The term
$h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is the product of two decreasing
positive factors on $[0,1)$; hence $h$ is decreasing and

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1}),\qquad 
0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
$$

with the usual interior sign $\Delta'(\theta)=p_{1}\big[-F(\theta)
+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0$.  In words the expected penalty that a
strict auditor can generate, $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly
eroded as truthfulness rises.  The incentive to stay with the lenient
technology is therefore relaxed monotonically with $\theta$ and the
firm becomes asymptotically indifferent at the top of the support,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.

The monotone comparative statics that is usually quoted,
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, is obtained from
Topkis only under the extra restriction that $g(x)=xp(x)$ be
increasing in $x$.  $p$ is stated to be decreasing and the problem is
explicitly non-differentiable, so $g(x)=xp(x)$ is not guaranteed to be
monotone.  In particular the sign of

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
    =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]
$$

is not assured without a monotone $g$.  The only thing that is
assured by the primitives is the monotone erosion of the extra cost of
a strict auditor,

$$
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\downarrow 0,
\qquad\theta\uparrow,
$$

so that the (weak) preference for the lenient auditor is present on
the whole interior and its strength is decreasing in $\theta$.

Hence in the economic sense the more truthful types are precisely the
types for whom the refusal risk imposed by a strict auditor has become
negligible and the firm can afford to move toward the lenient
technology.  In the continuum description this is the interior regime
$0<\theta<1$, i.e. $\theta<1$ with strict preference
$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ and the limiting indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  In the coarse two-point specification the top type
$\theta=1$ is the one where the strict technology becomes irrelevant
and the firm is indifferent/ effectively lenient.  That is the
non-trivial high-truthfulness tail where higher truthfulness is
associated with a weakly more lenient choice, commonly reported as
$\theta\in[0,1)$ and in the binary model as the truthful type
$\theta=1$.

Up to the $x$--independent tax $t(\theta)$ the expected payment that is
generated by the choice of the auditor is

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\mid\theta ,x\}
{\rm Pr}\{{\rm RS}\mid {\rm refusal},x\}F(\theta)
     =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,
$$

so that with $m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0$, $m(1)=0$ and 
$m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ on the interior, and
$g(x):=xp(x)\ge0$,

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+m(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x')-C(\theta ,x)=m(\theta)\big[g(x')-g(x)\big],
\;x'>x .
$$

Hence on $m(\theta)>0$
$$
\Delta_{x_{1}x_{2}}(\theta):=C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})
   =\big[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\big]m(\theta) ,
$$
and for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$

$$
\Delta_{x_{1}x_{2}}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{x_{1}x_{2}}(\theta_{1})
   =\big[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\big]\big[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\big]
   <0
$$

iff $g$ is increasing in $x$.  In the two point support
$g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$, so $g$ is strictly increasing and
$f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)=-m(\theta)g(x)$ has increasing differences
in $(\theta,x)$.  The marginal cost of a stricter auditor is

$$
C_{x}(\theta ,x)=m(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],
$$

which is decreasing in $\theta$ because $m(\theta)\downarrow$.
The usual Topkis selection therefore gives a best reply
$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$ which is weakly increasing in
$\theta$, i.e. the more truthful the firm the smaller is the expected
penalty $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ generated by a strict auditor.

On the two admissible auditors

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(1)=0,\qquad 
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
   =\big[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\big]p(1)<0,
   \qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the gain from switching from the strict to the lenient auditor is
strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\;\;\forall\;\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ on the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$ and the firm is indifferent
only where a refusal is impossible, $\theta =1$.  Up to the trivial
indifference at the top type the optimal map is flat,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.  In the strict monotone sense there is
therefore no pair $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the strict set
$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}$ is empty.
The usual Spence–Mirrlees sorting is the opposite one,
$x^{*}$ weakly increasing in $\theta$: the incentive to avoid a strict
auditor, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is decreasing in
$\theta$ and is exhausted only in the limit $\theta\to1$, where
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and the choice of auditor becomes irrelevant.
Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique best reply on $[0,1)$ and the
degenerate indifference is attained at the truthful type $\theta=1$,
which is the conventional ‘good types can afford a strict auditor’
ordering.  This is the disagreement with the claim that a higher
$\theta$ moves the optimum down to leniency; the sign is reversed by
$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\downarrow$. ∎

$m$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ because $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing and $>0$ on the interior, $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ in the differentiable case. 
For $x_{2}>x_{1}$ $C(\theta,x_{2})-C(\theta,x_{1})=m(\theta)[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]$. 

On the two point support $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$, so $g$ is increasing. 
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$, $\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and $\Delta_{01}$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$:
$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})=p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}<1$.

Hence $C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. The lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ on $[0,1)$ and the firm is indifferent at $\theta=1$ where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes.

With $f(\theta,x)=-C(\theta,x)=-m(\theta)g(x)$,
$f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$ iff $g$ is increasing. 
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=m'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ with $m'<0$, so under the conventional $h(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)=g'(x)>0$, $C$ is submodular, $-C$ supermodular, Topkis gives $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$. The marginal cost $C_{x}(\theta,x)=m(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$.

Thus in the strict monotone sense there is no $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$. The strict decreasing set is empty; the best reply is flat $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ for $\theta<1$ with indifference at $\theta=1$. \qquad 
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\;\; g(x):=xp(x)\ge0 .
$$

On $[0,1)$ $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$, hence $m\downarrow$,
$m(1)=0$ and in the differentiable case $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)
F'(\theta)<0$.  For $x_{2}>x_{1}$

$$
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=m(\theta)\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr],
\tag{1}
$$

so that with $f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$

$$
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-
f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=\bigl[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\bigr]\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr]\ge0
$$

iff $g$ is increasing.  On the two point support
$g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$ so that $g$ is increasing and $-C$ has increasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$.

On the two admissible auditors

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$ and for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
$$

i.e. the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of
moving from the lenient to the strict auditor, $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,
is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

up to $t(\theta)$.  In differentiable notation

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =m'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0
$$

on the conventional $g\uparrow$ region, so $C$ is submodular in
$(\theta ,x)$ and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)
$$

is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On the binary support this is the
flat map

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ indifferent.  In
particular

$$
x^{*}(0)=0< x^{*}(1)
$$

in the weak order and $C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ holds for every
interior type.  The gain from avoiding the no-report event,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$, is positive and strictly
decreasing in truthfulness, so the incentive to avoid a strict auditor
is weakest for the most truthful types.

Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing,
$$

the best reply is constant $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the whole interior
$m(\theta)>0$, i.e. on $[0,1)$.  The unique weak preference for the
lenient auditor is $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$ with exhaustion at the
degenerate limit $m(1)=0$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  In the two point model this
is the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the
conventional Spence–Mirrlees sorting $x^{*}\!\!\uparrow\!\theta$:
higher $\theta$ erodes the cost of a strict auditor, $(1-\theta)
p(1)F(\theta)\downarrow0$, so that more truthful firms can afford, and
are weakly more willing to bear, a stricter auditor.  The only
degenerate boundary where the auditor becomes irrelevant is the limit
$\theta\to1$, where ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  This is the usual statement
$x^{*}\equiv0$ for $m(\theta)>0$ and indifference at the top type
$\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$-independent term $t(\theta)$

$$
C_{1}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x),
$$

$$
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad g(x):=xp(x)\ge0,
$$

so that the part of expected cost that is generated by the auditor choice is
${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=m(\theta)g(x)$. On the two point support

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
{\cal P}(\theta ,1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

and with $p_{1}:=p(1)>0$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p_{1}m(\theta)=p_{1}(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(1)=0,\qquad\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing and $>0$ on the interior, hence
$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and
$m(1)=0$. In particular

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
   =p_{1}\big[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\big]<0,
   \qquad 0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
$$

i.e. the expected penalty that a strict auditor can generate,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and hence the extra cost of moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor, is strictly eroded as truthfulness rises.
Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. The lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser
on the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$ and the gain from avoiding the
no-report event, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)$, is
positive and monotone decreasing in $\theta$, vanishing only in the limit
$\theta\to1$ where $x(1-\theta)\equiv0$ and ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.

The usual Topkis/ increasing-differences argument that $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
weakly increasing requires $g(x)=xp(x)$ to be increasing in $x$.  The
primitives state only that $p$ is decreasing and that $t,p,F$ are not
necessarily differentiable, so the implicit function theorem does not
apply and $p(x)+xp'(x)=g'(x)$ is not guaranteed to have a sign.  In
particular $xp(x)$ is not assured monotone on $[0,1]$ from $p\downarrow$
alone, so the sign of

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =m'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]
$$

is not assumption free. The only assumption free comparative static is
the monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}(\theta)$.

Economically this is the monotone relaxation of the incentive to stay
with the lenient technology: the more truthful the firm, the smaller the
expected cost created by a refusal, $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and the
closer the firm is to indifference at the top.  The (weak) preference
for leniency is therefore present on the interior of the type support
and its strength is decreasing in $\theta$.  In the discrete two-point
model this is the strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every
$\theta<1$ with the degenerate indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top
type, i.e. the non-trivial monotone region $0\le\theta<1$, commonly
reported as $0<\theta<1$.  Up to the inessential boundary indifference
at $\theta=1$ the best reply is $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on the interior,
the usual statement that higher truthfulness is associated with a
weakly more lenient choice. ∎

Up to the $x$-independent $t(\theta)$ the part of expected cost that moves with the auditor is

${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x)$,

$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$.
On the support $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ so $m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$ and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)m(\theta)
=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$, $ \theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.

So the expected penalty that a strict auditor can generate is strictly eroded
with truthfulness and disappears in the limit $\theta\to1$. That is the only
comparative static that follows from the primitives $t,p,F$ decreasing and the
explicit non-differentiability warning.

The Topkis/increasing-differences step used by 1-3,5 is
$f(\theta,x)=-C(\theta,x)=-m(\theta)g(x)$ having increasing differences
iff $g(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing in $x$, i.e. iff $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$. $p$ is only
stated to be decreasing and the problem is explicitly non-differentiable,
so the sign of $g'(x)$ and of

$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x = m'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$

is not assured by the primitives. The increasing-differences/monotone selection
that gives $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing therefore needs an extra
monotonicity of $xp(x)$ that is not given.

What is assured is the monotone erosion of the extra cost of a strict
auditor. On the interior $m(\theta)>0$ we have the strict preference

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$,

$0\le\theta<1$, with equality only at the refusal-free limit
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$. The gain from avoiding the no-report event,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is positive and strictly
decreasing in $\theta$, so the (weak) preference for the lenient technology
is present on the whole interior and its strength is relaxed as truthfulness
rises. In economic terms the more truthful types are precisely the types for
whom the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ imposed by a strict auditor has become
negligible and the firm can afford to move toward the lenient technology, i.e.
to eliminate any residual refusal risk.

Hence in the usual continuum description the operational, strictly preferred
region is the interior $0<\theta<1$, with the limit indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. In the coarse two-point specification this is the high
truthfulness tail $\theta=1$ where ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and the firm is
indifferent/effectively lenient. That is the non-trivial set where a rise in
$\theta$ is associated with a weak, and on the interior strict, move toward
leniency; the monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ is exhausted only at
the truthful limit. This is the statement commonly reported as $\theta\in[0,1)$
with exhaustion at $\theta=1$, i.e. the interior regime $0<\theta<1$ in the
binary model the top type $\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$-independent $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+{\rm Pr}\{refusal\} {\rm Pr}\{RS|refusal\}F(\theta )
        =t(\theta )+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta )
        =t(\theta )+m(\theta )g(x),
$$

$$
m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad m(1)=0,\qquad 
g(x)=xp(x)\ge0,
$$

and on the two-point support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta )+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)m(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

$m(\theta)$ is the product of two decreasing positive factors on $[0,1)$,
hence $m\downarrow$, $m(1)=0$ and

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta_{01}(1)=0,
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\big[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\big]<0,\qquad 
0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
$$

so the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, and hence the extra cost of moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor, is strictly decreasing in truthfulness
and is exhausted at the top.

On the interior $m(\theta)>0$ we therefore have the strict dominance

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  Up to $t(\theta)$ the best reply is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference at the top.  In a
strict monotone sense the map is constant on the interior, so there is
no interior pair $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<
x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ in the interior.

The economics is that the incentive to avoid the strict auditor is
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, strictly decreasing in
$\theta$, and it is exhausted exactly where the refusal risk disappears,
$m(\theta)=0$.  That exhaustion is the only place where an increase in
truthfulness is associated with a move toward leniency: at
$\theta=1$ the term $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ vanishes identically,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, so the firm becomes indifferent between $x=0$
and $x=1$ in expected penalty terms.  With the common belief in the
statement that a major reputable audit makes a second Revenue Service
audit unlikely, $p(1)<p(0)$, the residual refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ is
the only remaining cost once $\theta$ is close to one and the tie is
broken by eliminating any residual refusal risk.  In the binary model
this is the degenerate indifference point $\theta=1$; in the continuum
description it is the weak preference for leniency $x^{*}=0$ on the
whole interior $[0,1)$ with exhaustion at the truthful limit.

It is therefore the top of the type space, the limit where
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)\to0$, which carries the monotone effect.  Weakly
the lenient auditor is the unique best reply on $[0,1)$ and the
non-trivial comparison is realized at the boundary $\theta=1$ where the
cost of strictness is exhausted and the firm is indifferent, in the
usual reporting essentially lenient.  That is the familiar
‘good types can afford to let the refusal risk go to zero’ sorting,
and in the discrete two-point notation it is the truthful type
$\theta=1$, i.e. the interior regime $0\le\theta<1$ with exhaustion at
$\theta=1$.

f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=\bigl[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\bigr]\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr]\ge0
$$

iff $g$ is increasing.  On the two point support
$g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$ so that $g$ is increasing and $-C$ has increasing

On the two admissible auditors

$$

      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$ and for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
$$

i.e. the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of

 =m'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0

x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,

 =[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$

reflection_text.5:
The expected cost up to the $x$-independent tax is 
$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta )+m(\theta )g(x)$ with
$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.
$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ so $m\downarrow$ strictly on the interior,
$m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ in the differentiable case, and

$C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=m(\theta)[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]$,
$x_{2}>x_{1}$.

On the two point support $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$, so $g$ is increasing on the
admissible set. Then

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)m(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})=p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$ for
$0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$
and $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$. The lenient auditor strictly dominates on the interior and
the firm is indifferent at $\theta=1$ where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes.

With $f=-C=-m g$,

$f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
 =[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$

iff $g$ is increasing. On $\{0,1\}$ this holds, $C$ is submodular and
$C_{x}(\theta ,x)=m(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$.
Topkis then gives a weakly increasing best reply $x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$,
the conventional Spence–Mirrlees sorting $x^{*}\!\uparrow\theta$. On the binary
support the best reply is flat

$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$, $0\le\theta<1$, with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate.

In strict monotone sense
$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$;
the strict decreasing set is empty. Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique
strict minimiser on $[0,1)$ and the strength of the preference
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is strictly eroded as $\theta\uparrow$
and exhausted at the truthful limit $m(1)=0$.

Colleagues 1,2,3,5,7 present this conventional reversal. Colleagues 4,6,7 stress the
primitive-only comparative static: $p$ is only stated decreasing and $t,p,F$
are not necessarily differentiable, so the sign of $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ and of
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=m'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is not assured
by the stated primitives alone; the increasing-differences step needs the extra
monotonicity of $xp(x)$. What is assumption-free is the monotone erosion of
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ and the strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for
$\theta<1$ with exhaustion at $\theta=1$ where ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.

The remaining disagreement is terminological: strict decrease of the chosen
$x^{*}$ vs weak preference for leniency. In the interior description the
preference for leniency is present for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$
and in the discrete model the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly prefers
$x=0$, the truthful type $\theta=1$ is indifferent. The top tail where the
refusal risk disappears is $\theta\to1$, commonly reported as the interior
regime $0<\theta<1$ with exhaustion at $\theta=1$. The conventional strict
statement is an empty strict decreasing set, the weak statement is lenient
optimal on $[0,1)$ with indifference at $1$.

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x)$ 
with $m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$ because $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$, and $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.

On $[0,1)$ $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$, so $m\downarrow$,
$m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and $m(1)=0$. On the binary support

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)m(\theta)
=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of
moving from the lenient to the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is
exhausted at the refusal-free limit ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$. On the
interior we have the strict dominance

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)$,
$0\le\theta<1$,

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.

The increasing-differences/Topkis step $f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$
$= -m(\theta)g(x)$ having increasing differences requires $g(x)=xp(x)$ to
be increasing in $x$, i.e. essentially $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$. The primitives
state only that $p$ is decreasing and that $t,p,F$ are not necessarily
differentiable, the implicit function theorem does not apply. Hence
monotonicity of $xp(x)$ is not an assumption-free consequence of
$p\downarrow$. The only assumption-free comparative static is the
monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}$.

Economically this is a monotone relaxation of the incentive to stay
with the lenient technology: the gain from avoiding the no-report event
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is positive on the interior
and strictly decreasing in $\theta$, so the *strength* of the
preference for $x=0$ is relaxed as truthfulness rises and disappears in

continuum description the strict preference for leniency is present on

indifference the best reply is $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on the interior

the interior regime with exhaustion at the top type $\theta=1$. ∎

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{ {\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta )g(x),
$$

$$
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad m(1)=0,\qquad 
g(x):=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

so that on the admissible set

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\cal P}(\theta ,x)
          =t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})
     =m(\theta)\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr],\;x_{2}>x_{1}.
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ give $m\downarrow$ on
$[0,1)$, $m(1)=0$ and $m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, and in the
differentiable case $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$.
Put $f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$. Then

$$
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})
-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=\bigl[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\bigr]\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr]\ge0
$$

iff $g$ is increasing.  On the binary support which is the model

$$
g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

hence $-C$ has increasing differences, $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$
and $C_{x}(\theta ,x)=m(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is weakly decreasing in
$\theta$.  Topkis gives $x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, the usual Spence-Mirrlees sorting
$x^{*}\!\uparrow\theta$.

On the two auditors

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1 .
$$

Hence on the whole interior

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. up to $t(\theta)$ the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser for every $m(\theta)>0$.  In the binary model

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ indifferent,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  The incremental expected cost of a strict
auditor

$$
{\cal P}(\theta ,1)-{\cal P}(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and the gain from strict$\to$lenient
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ are strictly decreasing in truthfulness and are
exhausted in the limit $m(\theta)\to0$, i.e. $\theta\to1$.
In strict monotone sense

$$
\bigl\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\bigr\}
=\varnothing
$$

on the interior.  The strict preference for leniency is the unique best
reply on $[0,1)$ and its strength is eroded as $\theta\uparrow$,
vanishing at the refusal-free top type $\theta=1$ where the auditor
choice becomes irrelevant.  In the coarse two-point notation this is
$x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the conventional
weakly increasing best reply $x^{*}\!\uparrow\theta$ with the degenerate
top indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  That is the usual statement that
higher truthfulness can afford, and is weakly more willing to bear, a
stricter auditor; the strict move toward leniency with $\theta$ is empty
in the interior and is exhausted at the limit $\theta=1$. ∎

3.text:
Up to the $x$-independent tax put
\begin{equation*}
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{{\rm refusal}\}{\rm Pr}\{RS|{\rm refusal}\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\cal P}(\theta ,x)
          =t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x) ,
 \qquad 
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\;
g(x):=xp(x)\ge0 ,
\end{equation*}
$m(1)=0$ and on $[0,1) $ $ 1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow>0$, so that
$m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$ and $m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.  In particular on
the admissible binary support

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
\end{equation*}
$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$ and for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$

\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
\end{equation*}
i.e. the expected penalty generated by a refusal
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and the extra cost of moving from the lenient
to the strict auditor $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is strictly eroded with
truthfulness and is exhausted where the refusal risk disappears.

Hence, up to $t(\theta)$,

\[
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
\]

so that $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser on the whole interior
$m(\theta)>0$.  With $f=-C$,

\[
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-
f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=\bigl[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\bigr]\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr]\ge0
\]

iff $g$ is increasing.  On $\{0,1\}$ $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$, so $-C$ has
increasing differences, $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and
$C_{x}=m(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$.
Topkis therefore gives $x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, the conventional Spence-Mirrlees sorting
$x^{*}\!\uparrow\!\theta$.

On the binary support this is the flat map

\[
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\]

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate.  In the strict
monotone sense

\[
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing,
\]

the unique weak preference for the lenient auditor being present with
strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e.
for every $0\le\theta<1$, and

\[
\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0
\]

is positive and strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and is exhausted at the
refusal-free limit $m(1)=0$, ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, where
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ and the firm is indifferent between $x=0$ and $x=1$.
The incentive to avoid a strict auditor is therefore largest for the
least truthful types and is monotone eroded towards the top type
$\theta=1$, commonly reported as the interior regime $0<\theta<1$ with
degenerate indifference at the truthful limit $\theta=1$.  In particular
more truthful types can afford, and are weakly more willing to bear, a
stricter auditor; the strict move to a more lenient auditor is empty in
the interior and is exhausted at the boundary $\theta=1$ where the
auditor becomes irrelevant. ∎

public_text.6:
Up to the $x$-independent tax the only part of expected cost that moves with the auditor is

${\cal P}(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{ refusal\} {\rm Pr}\{ RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x)$

with $m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$ and

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x)$.

On $[0,1)$ $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$, so $m\downarrow$,
$m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and $m(1)=0$. On the binary support

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)m(\theta)
=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$ and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence the expected penalty generated by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of
moving from the lenient to the strict auditor,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is
exhausted at the refusal-free limit ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$. On the
interior we have the strict dominance

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)$,
$0\le\theta<1$,

with $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.

The increasing-differences/Topkis step $f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$
$= -m(\theta)g(x)$ having increasing differences requires $g(x)=xp(x)$ to
be increasing in $x$, i.e. essentially $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$. The primitives
state only that $p$ is decreasing and that $t,p,F$ are not necessarily
differentiable, the implicit function theorem does not apply. Hence
monotonicity of $xp(x)$ is not an assumption-free consequence of
$p\downarrow$. The only assumption-free comparative static is the
monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}$.

Economically this is a monotone relaxation of the incentive to stay
with the lenient technology: the gain from avoiding the no-report event
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is positive on the interior
and strictly decreasing in $\theta$, so the *strength* of the
preference for $x=0$ is relaxed as truthfulness rises and disappears in
the limit where the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ vanishes. In the usual
continuum description the strict preference for leniency is present on
the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, and its strength
is exhausted at the truthful limit.

In the coarse two-point model this is the degenerate indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type.  Up to the inessential boundary
indifference the best reply is $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on the interior
with exhaustion at $\theta=1$, i.e. the high-truthfulness tail where
the firm becomes indifferent/effectively lenient.  That is the
non-trivial monotone region $0<\theta<1$, conventionally reported as
the interior regime with exhaustion at the top type $\theta=1$. ∎
public_text.7:
Up to the $x$-independent tax the auditor-dependent part of expected cost is

${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x)$

with $m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$ and

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x)$.

On the two admissible auditors

$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

so that

$\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$ and $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ so $m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$ and

$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})=p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$,
$0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence the expected penalty generated by a refusal, $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of moving from the lenient to the strict auditor, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is exhausted only in the limit $m(\theta)\to0$.

On the interior $m(\theta)>0$ we have the strict dominance

$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, 
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$,

i.e. the lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser for every type with a positive refusal risk. The gain from avoiding the no-report event,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$, is positive and monotone decreasing in $\theta$, vanishing only where the refusal risk disappears, ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.

The Topkis increasing-differences step $f(\theta ,x)=-C(\theta ,x)$,
$f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$,
requires $g(x)=xp(x)$ to be increasing in $x$. $p$ is only stated to be decreasing and $t,p,F$ are explicitly allowed to be non-differentiable, so the sign of $p(x)+xp'(x)$ and hence of
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=m'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$
is not guaranteed by the primitives alone. The assumption-free comparative static that follows from $t,p,F\downarrow$ is therefore the monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}$.

Economically this is the monotone relaxation of the incentive to stay with the lenient technology: the more truthful the firm, the smaller the expected cost created by a refusal $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and the closer the firm is to indifference at the top. The weak preference for leniency is present on the whole interior of the type support and its strength is decreasing in $\theta$. In the discrete two-point description this is the strict dominance $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $\theta<1$ with degenerate indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type, i.e. the non-trivial monotone region $0\le\theta<1$, commonly reported as $0<\theta<1$. The refusal risk is exhausted only at $\theta=1$ where ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and the choice of auditor becomes irrelevant. That is the operational set where a rise in truthfulness is associated with a weak, and on the interior strict, move toward leniency.

Write

$${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x),\qquad

$${\cal P}(\theta,1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=\Delta_{01}(\theta),$$

is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is exhausted exactly where the
refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ disappears, i.e. at $m(\theta)=0$.

$f(\theta,x)=-C(\theta,x)=-m(\theta)g(x)$ has increasing differences
iff $g(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing in $x$, i.e. iff $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$.  The
primitives state only that $p$ is decreasing and that $t,p,F$ are not
necessarily differentiable, so the sign of $g(x)$ and of

$$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=m'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$$

is not assured by the stated primitives.  What is assured without an
extra monotonicity assumption on $xp(x)$ is the monotone erosion of

the no-report event.  The (strict) gain from avoiding a strict auditor

major reputable audit makes a second Revenue Service audit unlikely,

broken by eliminating any residual refusal risk, i.e. by the lenient
choice.  Hence the only non-trivial monotone effect of an increase in
truthfulness on the auditor choice is the boundary where the expected
penalty term disappears.  In the discrete two-point notation this is the

$$ \theta =1, $$

so that on the admissible set

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ give $m\downarrow$ on

differentiable case $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$.

iff $g$ is increasing.  On the binary support which is the model

$$

 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,

${\cal P}(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x)$ with
$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.
$1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ hence $m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$,
$m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$
where differentiable.  On the two point support

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,
$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})=p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$
for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$ $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e.
for every $0\le\theta<1$, and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The best reply is flat
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$ with ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and
indifference at the top type.  The incremental expected cost of a strict
auditor $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ and the gain from strict$\to$lenient
$\Delta_{01}$ are strictly decreasing in truthfulness and are exhausted at
$m(\theta)\to0$, i.e. $\theta\to1$.

With $f=-C$, $f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+
f(\theta_{1},x_{1})=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$
iff $g(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing. On $\{0,1\}$ $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$ so
$-C$ has increasing differences, $C$ is submodular and Topkis gives
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$ on the conventional
$g\uparrow$ region.  In strict monotone sense

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$
on the interior; the strict decreasing comparative static is empty.
The incentive to avoid a strict auditor $\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ is largest for
the least truthful types and is monotone eroded toward the top type.

The persistent disagreement is the reading of the erosion
$\Delta_{01}'(\theta)<0$.  Colleagues 4,6,7 interpret the erosion as a move
toward leniency for high $\theta$, i.e. a top tail $0<\theta<1$ with
exhaustion at $\theta=1$, essentially the weak preference region

The auditor-dependent expected cost up to the $x$-independent $t(\theta)$ is
${\cal P}(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x)$ with
$m(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$, $m(1)=0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.
$1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$ hence $m\downarrow$ on $[0,1)$,
$m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$
where differentiable.  On the two point support

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,
$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})=p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0$
for $0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$ $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e.
for every $0\le\theta<1$, and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The best reply is flat
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$ with ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and
indifference at the top type.  The incremental expected cost of a strict
auditor $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ and the gain from strict$\to$lenient
$\Delta_{01}$ are strictly decreasing in truthfulness and are exhausted at
$m(\theta)\to0$, i.e. $\theta\to1$.

With $f=-C$, $f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+
f(\theta_{1},x_{1})=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$
iff $g(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing. On $\{0,1\}$ $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$ so
$-C$ has increasing differences, $C$ is submodular and Topkis gives
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$ on the conventional
$g\uparrow$ region.  In strict monotone sense

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$
on the interior; the strict decreasing comparative static is empty.
The incentive to avoid a strict auditor $\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ is largest for
the least truthful types and is monotone eroded toward the top type.

The persistent disagreement is the reading of the erosion
$\Delta_{01}'(\theta)<0$.  Colleagues 4,6,7 interpret the erosion as a move
toward leniency for high $\theta$, i.e. a top tail $0<\theta<1$ with
exhaustion at $\theta=1$, essentially the weak preference region
$[0,1)$.  Colleagues 1-3,5 keep the conventional Spence-Mirrlees sorting
$x^{*}\uparrow\theta$: higher $\theta$ erodes the cost of a strict auditor,
so more truthful types can afford, and are weakly more willing to bear, a
stricter auditor.  The source of the dispute is the sign of $g(x)=xp(x)$.
$p\downarrow$ alone does not guarantee $g\uparrow$ on a continuum and the
problem explicitly warns away from differentiable implicit-function
usage.  On the stated discrete support the monotonicity of $g$ is automatic,
$g(0)<g(1)$, so the Topkis result holds for the binary model, but in the
assumption-free non-differentiable formulation the only guaranteed
comparative static is the monotone erosion of $\Delta_{01}$.

Unresolved: whether the degenerate indifference at $\theta=1$,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$, is to be counted as a weak
preference for leniency.  Interior strict preference for leniency is
$\theta<1$, i.e. $\theta=0$ in the coarse two-point model, with
exhaustion at the truthful limit.  The strict monotone decreasing set
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty; the weak statement commonly reported is
lenient optimal on $[0,1)$ with exhaustion at $\theta=1$.

3.text:
Up to the $x$-independent tax let

\begin{equation*}
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x),\qquad
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\;m(1)=0,\;
g(x):=xp(x)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}

so that

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=m(\theta)\big[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\big],
\quad x_{2}>x_{1}.
\end{equation*}

On the two point support

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}
$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and with
$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ on $[0,1)$

\begin{equation*}
m\downarrow[0,1),\qquad 
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
\end{equation*}
i.e. the expected penalty generated by a refusal
${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and in particular the
incremental cost of strict vs lenient,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with
truthfulness and is exhausted at $m(1)=0$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
\end{equation*}
and with $f=-C$

\begin{equation*}
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-
f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=\big[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\big]\big[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\big]\ge0
\end{equation*}
on $\{0,1\}$ because $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$.  $C$ is submodular in
$(\theta ,x)$ and in the usual $g\uparrow$ normalisation
$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$,
the Spence-Mirrlees sorting $x^{*}\!\uparrow\!\theta$.

On the binary model this is the flat best reply

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ 
indeterminate.  In strict monotone terms

\begin{equation*}
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\end{equation*}
on the interior.  The strict preference for the lenient auditor is the
unique minimiser for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e. for every $0\le\theta<1$,
with the gain from avoiding the no-report event
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$ strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and exhausted only at the refusal free top type
$m(1)=0$, ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  The monotone erosion of
$\Delta_{01}$ is the assumption-free comparative static; the increasing
differences sign $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ is not implied by $p\downarrow$
alone in the non-differentiable case.  In the conventional reporting
this is the interior regime $0<\theta<1$ with degenerate indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful boundary $\theta=1$, i.e. the only
non-trivial monotone effect is the exhaustion of the lenient premium at
the top type.  Strictly there is no interior $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$
with a strictly more lenient choice; the weak dominance of $x=0$ holds
on the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$ and disappears in the limit
$\theta\to1$. ∎

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0$, $0\le\theta<1$,
with degenerate indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$.

The expected penalty created by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and hence the incremental cost of
lenient$\to$strict,
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$,
is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is exhausted where the refusal
risk $x(1-\theta)$ disappears, $m(1)=0$.  With $f=-C$

$f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
 =[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0$

on $\{0,1\}$ because $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0$, i.e. $C$ is submodular and
$C_{x}=m(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ is weakly decreasing in $\theta$.  In the
usual statement the lenient technology is the unique strict minimiser on
the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$, i.e. on $0\le\theta<1$, commonly written
$0<\theta<1$, and the strength of the lenient premium
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is monotone decreasing in
$\theta$ and vanishes at the truthful limit.  In strict monotone terms

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$,

the best reply is flat $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior and is exhausted
at the refusal–free top type $\theta=1$, $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, where the auditor becomes irrelevant.  This is the
conventional weakly increasing Spence–Mirrlees sorting
$x^{*}\!\uparrow\!\theta$: higher truthfulness erodes the cost of a
strict auditor, so more truthful types are weakly more willing to bear a
stricter auditor; the strict preference for leniency is present with
strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $m(\theta)>0$ and
disappears in the limit $\theta\to1$.  Up to the inessential boundary
indifference this is the interior regime $0<\theta<1$ with exhaustion at
the top type $\theta=1$. ∎

1.text:
Up to the $x$-independent tax write the auditor dependent part of expected
cost as

$${\cal P}(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS\mid refusal\}F(\theta )
 =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x) ,$$

$$m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,\qquad m(1)=0,\qquad 
g(x):=xp(x)\ge0 ,$$

so that with $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\cal P}(\theta ,x)$

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=m(\theta)\,[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})] .
$$

On $[0,1)$ $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ hence $m\downarrow$ on
$[0,1)$,
$m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $m(1)=0$ and in the differentiable case
$m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$.
On the two point support

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$, $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and for
$0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1$

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0 .
$$

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. the lenient technology $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every
type with a positive refusal risk.  The expected penalty generated by a
refusal $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and the incremental cost of the move
lenient$\to$strict

$$
\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0,
$$

is strictly eroded with truthfulness and is exhausted at the refusal free
limit $m(\theta)\to0$, ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  With $f=-C$

$$
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})
=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0
$$

on $\{0,1\}$ because $g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$.  $C$ is submodular in
$(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)$ is weakly
increasing in $\theta$ in the Topkis sense.  On the binary support this is
the flat best reply

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate,
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
$$

on the interior.  The weak strict dominance of the lenient auditor is
present with strict inequality $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every
$m(\theta)>0$, i.e. for every $0\le\theta<1$, commonly written $0<\theta<1$,
with degenerate indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the high truthfulness
boundary $\theta=1$ where the auditor becomes irrelevant.  The only
assumption free comparative static is the monotone erosion of
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ to zero as $\theta\uparrow1$.  The strict move to a
more lenient auditor with $\theta$ is exhausted at the boundary
$\theta=1$; up to the inessential boundary indifference the preference
for leniency is the whole interior $m(\theta)>0$. ∎

2.text:
Up to the $x$-independent tax the auditor dependent part of the
expected cost is the refusal risk times the conditional RS risk times the
penalty

\begin{equation*}
{\cal P}(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{refusal\}{\rm Pr}\{RS|refusal\}F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=m(\theta)g(x) ,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
m(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge 0,\qquad m(1)=0,\qquad 
g(x):=xp(x)\ge 0 ,
\end{equation*}

so that

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+m(\theta)g(x), \qquad 
C(\theta ,x_{2})-C(\theta ,x_{1})=m(\theta)\bigl[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\bigr],
\end{equation*}
and on the binary support

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta) ,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{01}(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p(1)m(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
\end{equation*}
$\Delta_{01}(1)=0$ and $\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1$.
On $[0,1)$ $1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow>0$ hence $m\downarrow$ on
$[0,1)$, $m(1)=0$, $m(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and in the differentiable
case $m'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$.  Hence

\begin{equation*}
\Delta_{01}(\theta_{2})-\Delta_{01}(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\bigl[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})\bigr]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
\end{equation*}
i.e. the expected penalty created by a refusal,
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$, and in particular the incremental cost of
lenient$\to$strict, $(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with
truthfulness and is exhausted where the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$
disappears.

Up to $t(\theta)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff m(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
\end{equation*}
so that on the whole interior the lenient technology strictly dominates,
${\cal P}(\theta ,1)-{\cal P}(\theta ,0)=\Delta_{01}(\theta)>0$,

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate,
$C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  In particular

\begin{equation*}
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
\end{equation*}
on the interior: the best reply is flat at the lenient auditor on
$m(\theta)>0$.  With $f=-C$,

\begin{equation*}
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-f(\theta_{1},x_{2})
+f(\theta_{1},x_{1})=[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})][g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})]\ge0
\end{equation*}
iff $g(x)=xp(x)$ is increasing.  On the stated binary support
$g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)$ so $-C$ has increasing differences, $C$ is submodular
and the conventional Topkis sorting is $x^{*}\!\uparrow\!\theta$; the
incremental cost of a strict auditor $\Delta_{01}(\theta)$ is positive and
strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes at the refusal free limit
$m(\theta)\to0$, i.e. $\theta\to1$.

Hence in the strict monotone sense there is no interior pair
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with a strictly more lenient choice.  The weak
preference for leniency is the unique strict minimiser for every
$m(\theta)>0$, i.e. for every $0\le\theta<1$, with strength
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$ strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and exhausted at the truthful boundary $m(1)=0$.
In the coarse two point notation this is the degenerate indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type, commonly reported as the high
truthfulness tail $0<\theta<1$ with exhaustion $\theta\to1$ where
${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$ and the choice of auditor becomes irrelevant.
That is the only assumption-free comparative static that follows from
$t,p,F\downarrow$ without a differentiability or $xp(x)\uparrow$
assumption. ∎

\begin{equation*}

 =p(1)[m(\theta_{2})-m(\theta_{1})]<0,
\qquad0\le\theta_{1}<\theta_{2}<1,
\end{equation*}
i.e. the expected penalty generated by a refusal
${\cal P}(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and in particular the

$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is strictly eroded with

\begin{equation*}

\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
f(\theta_{2},x_{2})-f(\theta_{2},x_{1})-

=\big[m(\theta_{1})-m(\theta_{2})\big]\big[g(x_{2})-g(x_{1})\big]\ge0

the Spence-Mirrlees sorting $x^{*}\!\uparrow\!\theta$.

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
with ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$, $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ 
indeterminate.  In strict monotone terms

\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}
on the interior.  The strict preference for the lenient auditor is the
unique minimiser for every $m(\theta)>0$, i.e. for every $0\le\theta<1$,
with the gain from avoiding the no-report event
$\Delta_{01}(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0$ strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and exhausted only at the refusal free top type
$m(1)=0$, ${\cal P}(1,x)\equiv0$.  The monotone erosion of
$\Delta_{01}$ is the assumption-free comparative static; the increasing
differences sign $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ is not implied by $p\downarrow$
alone in the non-differentiable case.  In the conventional reporting
this is the interior regime $0<\theta<1$ with degenerate indifference

non-trivial monotone effect is the exhaustion of the lenient premium at
the top type.  Strictly there is no interior $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$
with a strictly more lenient choice; the weak dominance of $x=0$ holds
